title: Regret at not studying more: Tuskegee, the conservatory, Prince Robinson's harmony books
summary: His only regret is not being a better-trained musician; a Tuskegee scholarship fell through, he passed up a Boston conservatory, and Prince Robinson left him harmony books before he could teach him.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Is there any part of it -- of your life -- that you would have changed?

Only to be a better musician. I would say. You know. Because I had a chance -- well, scholarship to Tuskegee, under Captain Dryer. He was the leader of the band at Tuskegee then, and something happened. I couldn't make it. I didn't get a chance to get in there, and later on in years I was in Boston, Massachusetts, there, and I had a chance to get in the conservatory there. That --

Well, I had many chances. I had a chance in Washington, D. C., in the Howard theater there, you know. I could have gone and studied music, and a few places I did have a teacher here, or a teacher there, but you know. I picked up what I could here from this one, and from that one, and like Prince Robinson, tenor saxaphone player, he was quite a musi-

cian, and he taught harmony, you know. And he -- I have some of his books. He -- you -- he left the books and things, his harmony books and things, to me. And he was supposed to take me on as student, and he passed before we could get together. You know?
And I'm sorry I missed that, from him. He said don't worry about it. I've got the books right here now. They were very expensive books, too.
But you never did actually do any studying, take any --
Yes, I did studying, but I mean I didn't do the studying that I --
That you would like to do.
Would have What I'd like to. Hell yes, I --
